title: Explain the corridor system
prompt: Explain the corridor system. Why does the interbank rate stay inside it?
quote: If there is the verb 'explain', it is not sufficient to draw three lines. You must say something and explain why it is really a corridor.
keyPoints: Names the three rates: marginal lending facility rate = ceiling, deposit facility rate = floor, MRO rate = policy rate in the middle
The overnight interbank rate oscillates around the MRO rate, because the central bank runs MROs continuously and supplies liquidity when it drifts
Ceiling: above it, a bank borrows from the central bank instead → interbank demand falls → rate falls back
Floor: below it, a bank with excess liquidity deposits at the central bank instead → interbank supply falls → rate rises back
Exception: in a severe crisis (2007–08) the rate can exceed the ceiling if the central bank does not open the window / supply liquidity
Signal: the level of the rates (up = more restrictive) and the width (narrow = less fluctuation tolerated)

title: Term structure: forward rates and the upward slope
prompt: Explain the expectations theory of the term structure. How do you obtain the forward rates implicit in the yield curve, and why is the curve usually upward-sloping?
quote: It is implicit in the yield curve the forward interest rate expected by the market. This is the typical question in the exam, because it is very easy to answer.
keyPoints: Expectations theory: the expected return of the strategies (roll over short vs hold long) is the same for any horizon; the long rate ≈ average of current and expected short rates
No-arbitrage argument: if (1+R)ⁿ > Π(1+rᵢ), borrow short and invest long → short rates rise, the long rate falls, until equality
Formula: 1 + rₙ = (1 + Rₙ)ⁿ / (1 + Rₙ₋₁)ⁿ⁻¹, and can apply it with numbers
The yield curve contains a structure of forward rates: it reflects market expectations
Limit: the curve is usually upward-sloping; pure expectations would need short rates expected to rise most of the time
What explains it: liquidity premium (Hicks: lenders prefer to lend short) and a risk element rising with maturity (Meiselman, Modigliani–Sutch: long prices vary more)
Inverted curves still happen (US 2005–07, 2019): read as expected crisis / short rates expected to be cut

title: Balance sheet and transactions-flow matrices
prompt: Describe the simple closed-economy stock-flow framework: what do the balance sheet and transactions-flow matrices show, and what are the key identities?
quote: I can ask you something about this balance sheet matrix and transaction matrix, some of the identities that I have shown you. They are very simple things, but they are very important.
where: 10_08 §§3–5 · exam flag [0:57]. The matrices in the notes are reconstructed: check the slides!
keyPoints: Stock vs flow; final stock = initial stock + revaluations + net acquisitions
Every financial asset is another sector's liability: financial rows sum to zero; only real capital K has no counterpart
Sectoral balances (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M): derived from Y = C + I + G + (X − M); an ex post identity, not causal (crowding out depends on whether output can change)
Net private wealth = K + B + H: public debt is private wealth (denied under Ricardian equivalence)
Transactions matrix: receipts/sources +, expenditures/acquisitions −; rows and columns sum to zero
I = ΔL (all profits distributed); government: G + r·B₋₁ − T = ΔB + ΔH; household saving = ΔD + ΔB_h
Stocks feed back on flows (interest on debt, wealth effects, Tobin's desired proportions)

title: Quantity theory: what ensures money market equilibrium?
prompt: In the quantity theory of money, what variable ensures equilibrium in the money market? Explain the mechanism.
quote: What is the variable that in the quantity theory of money ensures the equilibrium in the money market? It is the price level.
keyPoints: Answer: the price level P
MV = PT is an accounting identity; it becomes a theory by assuming V (institutional factors) and T/Y (potential output) given and independent, and M exogenous
Why T is given: Say's law (classical) or full employment through wage flexibility and factor substitution (marginalists)
Cambridge version: M_d = k·P·Y with k = 1/V; the public holds balances in proportion to income (transactions demand)
Mechanism: M_s rises → excess money balances → spending on goods; output is given → P rises → money market equilibrium restored
Both versions work through P: in real terms the real supply falls back; in nominal terms nominal demand k·P·Y rises
Causality runs M → P; with endogenous money it reverses. Money is neutral (a veil), with the classical dichotomy

title: Sidrauski: equilibrium conditions and their meaning
prompt: Present the Sidrauski model: its equilibrium conditions and their economic meaning.
quote: When we do the Sidrauski model, there are some equilibrium conditions that I would like you to know, because they have a precise economic meaning.
where: 10_06 §13, 10_08 §9, 10_20 §§7–9 · final exam only (not the midterm). Equilibrium conditions still to come: add them after the next lectures.
keyPoints: Why it exists: in long-run GE there is no reason to hold money (Hahn); Sidrauski puts money in the utility function (after Patinkin)
Money in the utility function removes the dichotomy, yet yields neutrality and even super-neutrality: money growth (inflation) doesn't affect real steady-state variables
Assumptions: infinite horizon, no uncertainty, no labour–leisure choice (else backward-bending supply, multiple equilibria), services of money proportional to m
u(c, m) increasing, strictly concave, separable over time; u_m → ∞ as m → 0 (some money held) and a finite satiation level m̄ (not too much)
Production y_t = f(k_{t−1}/(1+n)), constant returns, Inada conditions; the agent maximises Σ βᵗ u(c_t, m_t)
Budget constraint: income + transfers + undepreciated capital + [(1+i)b + m]/((1+π)(1+n)) = c + k + b + m
Its structure underlies the models used at central banks (New Keynesian models add rigidities)
[Add after class] the equilibrium conditions and what each one means economically

title: Tobin's portfolio choice: derive the risk–return profile
prompt: Present Tobin's portfolio choice between money and a risky asset. Derive the risk–return profile and show how a rise in the interest rate affects the demand for money.
quote: I can ask you to derive the risk–return profile. It is very simple. But you must do something else.
keyPoints: Tobin drops Keynes's definite expectation: the highest probability goes to r_e = r₀, so expected capital gain is 0 and risk is σ_g
Portfolio of money (share a₁, no return, no risk) and a risky security (share a₂ = 1 − a₁)
Expected return = a₂·r; risk σ_R = a₂·σ_g
Substituting a₂ = σ_R/σ_g: risk–return profile E(R) = (r/σ_g)·σ_R, a straight line
Risk-averse investor with convex indifference curves chooses the tangency point; a₂ = σ_R/σ_g gives the risky share
A rise in r rotates the profile up; if substitution beats income effect, the money share falls: inverse r–money-demand relation without corner solutions
Limits: lose Keynes's changing expectations; liquidity trap only in special cases (Modigliani: r near zero)

title: Kaldor vs Friedman: is a stable V proof of the quantity theory?
prompt: Friedman takes the stability of velocity as evidence for the quantity theory. Explain Kaldor's answer, and his criticism of Keynes.
quote: V is constant or stable only because M is 'unstable'. … This can be a question on the slides.
keyPoints: With endogenous money the central bank sets r*; the money supply is horizontal at r*
A rise in money demand (nominal income) raises M at the same r, so V stays unchanged
With exogenous M (Keynes's liquidity preference, IS-LM), higher income raises r and so V: velocity is not stable
Kaldor: V is stable only because M is 'unstable', i.e. M adapts to the demand for money; a stable V proves nothing about the quantity theory
Keynes and the monetarists both assume M exogenous; Keynes's exogenous M gave Friedman the V-stability test
Keynes erred by thinking in terms of commodity money (gold), whose supply can't adapt; in a credit economy excess balances are extinguished (repaying debt, buying interest-bearing assets)
Worked contrast with M·V(r) = Y: Friedman, M changes → nominal Y changes; Kaldor, Y changes → M adjusts at the given rate
